title: CaliDist: Calibrating Large Language Models via Behavioral Robustness to Distraction
claim: Model accuracy falls steadily as sensitivity to input perturbation rises, consistently across different models.
layout: 4 panels in a row, same axes, dual y-axis overlay on histogram
description: A single row of four panels (a–d), each for a different LLM: Llama-3.1, Qwen-3, Phi-4-Mini and Gemini-2.0-Flash. Each panel uses the same dataset (csqa) and the same distractor type (sample corruption). Each is a histogram of Prediction Instability (μ) on the x-axis, with five pink bars. The left y-axis is frequency in bin, and the count is printed above each bar. The tallest bar is at low μ and the bars shrink toward high μ. A dark green line with markers is overlaid on a right y-axis (0–1) showing accuracy in bin. It slopes downward from about 0.9 to about 0.3–0.45, and each point is labeled with its value in green. The eye goes first to the green declining line. The italic captions under the panels name the models.
caption: {Negative correlation between prediction accuracy and prediction instability.} Accuracy drops as Prediction Instability $\mu$ increases. Samples on which the models demonstrate higher $\mu$ tend to have lower average accuracy. Distractor used: Sample-corruption style.
abstract: Existing calibration methods for Large Language Models (LLMs) often overlook a critical dimension of trustworthiness: a model's behavioral robustness to irrelevant or misleading information. In this paper, we argue that a model's true confidence should reflect its stability under cognitive pressure. We introduce CaliDist, a novel post-hoc calibration approach that directly measures and penalizes a model's susceptibility to distraction. CaliDist quantifies how an LLM's predictions and uncertainty change when its input prompt is perturbed with semantic distractors. This stability (or lack thereof) signal is then used to adaptively scale the model's initial confidence score. Our extensive experiments on seven Natural Language Understanding classification benchmarks using six distinct LLMs show that CaliDist consistently achieves lower Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score compared with strong baselines. Remarkably, our method reduces the ECE from 23% to 7% on average--a relative improvement of 70%--demonstrating that behavioral stability is a powerful signal for calibration. We make our code and datasets available at github.com/anas-jawad/CaliDist.
